name: Kanto-Style Sukiyaki (Japanese Beef Hot Pot)
why: Peak hot-pot weather, and this is the most hands-on-skill Japanese pot dish there is: searing thin ribeye in beef suet, dipping everything in beaten raw egg, and finishing with udon in the enriched sauce. A natural next step after all the Korean experiments, with a silky egg-dipping technique you've never cooked before.
author: Henry
ingredients: For the warishita sauce: 120ml sake, 120ml mirin, 120ml soy sauce, 3 tbsp sugar
225g thinly sliced beef ribeye or chuck, sliced 2-3mm thick (sukiyaki-cut from a butcher, or freeze 30 min to slice thin)
1 tbsp neutral oil or 1 piece beef suet
4 napa cabbage leaves (~340g), cut into 2-inch pieces
White part of 2 large leeks, cut into 1/2-inch diagonal slices
100g baby spinach or chrysanthemum greens, cut into 2-inch pieces
2 shiitake mushrooms, stems removed, caps scored with a cross
~50g enoki mushrooms, root trimmed, separated into clusters
130g firm or grilled (yaki) tofu, cut into 1-inch pieces
100g shirataki noodles, blanched 2 minutes and drained (or skip)
120ml kombu dashi or water, for thinning the sauce
250g cooked udon noodles for the shime finish

steps: Combine sake and mirin in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil and simmer 30 seconds to evaporate the alcohol.
Add sugar and stir until dissolved. Add soy sauce, bring to a brief boil, then remove from heat and set aside — this is your warishita sauce.
Cut napa cabbage into 2-inch pieces. Slice leeks diagonally into 1/2-inch pieces.
Score shiitake caps with a cross, trim the enoki, cut tofu into 1-inch pieces, and blanch shirataki noodles for 2 minutes then drain.
Arrange all vegetables and tofu on a platter grouped by type; keep the sliced beef on a separate plate.
Crack one egg into each dipping bowl and break the yolk gently with chopsticks — loose and slightly streaky, not fully whisked.
Set a cast-iron pot or heavy skillet (with a handle you can hold) on the hob at medium heat. Add the oil or beef suet and let it melt and coat the bottom.
Lay a few slices of beef in a single layer. Sear about 30 seconds per side until lightly caramelized.
Dip the seared beef in the beaten egg and eat immediately — that's your first course.
Pour enough warishita into the pot to cover the bottom about 6mm deep. Arrange vegetables, tofu and shirataki in the sauce, grouped by type.
Simmer over medium-low for 5-7 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Transfer cooked items to your bowl, dip in egg and eat. Keep adding beef and vegetables as space opens up, adding more warishita as it reduces — thin with dashi or water if it gets too concentrated.
When everything's eaten, add the cooked udon noodles to the remaining warishita in the pot.
Simmer 2-3 minutes until the noodles are coated in the enriched, reduced sauce — this is the shime, the traditional finish.
Spoon into bowls and serve immediately, with any leftover egg for dipping.

pro_tips: Beef suet (fat) is the traditional Kanto frying medium and gives the caramelized beef a distinctly richer, beefier base than oil — worth asking a butcher for a small piece. If you can't get it, a neutral high-smoke-point oil works fine.

The egg dip is the whole point: sear the beef, dip, eat. Don't fully whisk the egg — a loose, streaky mix gives a silkier coating. And the shime (udon in the final sauce) is where all the reduced sweet-savoury flavour concentrates — never skip it.
